title: Subsea Umbilicals

Minimum bend radius and overbending analysis

Internal tube pressure and integrity analysis

models.text: The suite should implement axial elasticity, generalized Hooke's law, Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theories, cable catenary equations, Cosserat rod theory, nonlinear bending–torsion relationships, elastic rod theory, geometric nonlinearities and three-dimensional cable equilibrium.

The suite should include classical laminate theory where appropriate, multilayer composite beam models, helical wire mechanics, helical armour stress formulations, equivalent axial stiffness, equivalent bending stiffness, torsional stiffness, layer interaction models and contact mechanics for internal tubes, armour and fillers.

models.group: Internal tube pressure and collapse models
models.text: It should include thin- and thick-wall pressure vessel relationships, Lamé elasticity, pressure containment models, elastic instability, shell collapse theory, external pressure buckling, crush resistance, nonlinear contact and local deformation analysis.

The suite should implement Fourier heat conduction, Newton's law of cooling, transient thermal diffusion, thermal expansion relationships, coupled thermal stress, internal convective heat transfer and multilayer heat-transfer resistance models.

Models should include Morison's equation, wave-current kinematics, added-mass and drag formulations, vessel-motion response, dynamic cable finite elements, catenary lay geometry, minimum bend-radius relationships, touchdown-zone contact, nonlinear seabed friction and lowering-line dynamics.

The suite should incorporate S–N relationships, Palmgren–Miner damage, rainflow counting, local strain fatigue models, stress concentration factors, armour-wire fatigue, fretting fatigue, wear models, damage accumulation and reliability-based service-life assessment.

The suite should combine global cable dynamics with detailed multilayer finite-element cross-sectional analysis, nonlinear contact and friction with cyclic fatigue models, transient thermal analysis with mechanical stress response, and measured umbilical stiffness with numerical calibration. Hybrid reduced-order sectional models and high-fidelity three-dimensional finite-element models should be used to balance computational efficiency with local accuracy.

inputs.text: Total length, outside diameter, internal element arrangement, cross-sectional layup, armour configuration and helical lay angles.
Hydraulic tubes, electrical conductors, fibre-optic elements, fillers, strength members, armour layers and outer sheath.
Tensile stiffness, bending stiffness, density, elastic modulus, yield strength, thermal expansion and fatigue properties of constituent materials.
Tube diameters and wall thicknesses, conductor cross-sectional areas, fibre-optic package dimensions and insulation thicknesses.
Hydraulic operating pressure, test pressure, external hydrostatic pressure and internal tube pressure transients.
Fluid operating temperature, ambient seawater temperature, thermal conductivity and thermal expansion characteristics.
Route length, water depth, seabed profile, installation vessel geometry, lay tension, overboarding radius and deployment sequence.
Hang-off elevation, top-end vessel motion, buoyancy elements, lazy-wave geometry where applicable and end-termination restraints.
Wave conditions, current profiles, drag coefficients, added-mass coefficients and seawater density.
Soil stiffness, seabed friction, embedment, seabed roughness and contact resistance.
Minimum bend radius, allowable tension, maximum compressive loading, crushing capacity and termination ratings.
Stress concentration factors, cyclic loading spectra, material fatigue characteristics and expected operating cycles.
Termination geometry, connection stiffness, distribution unit locations and umbilical support structures.
Design life, internal pressure cycles, operating temperature cycles and expected inspection conditions.

subtitle: Dynamic umbilicals, static umbilicals, internal functional elements, installation, bending, fatigue and pressure integrity.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the umbilical's installed or deployment-stage geometry, including the overall centreline, hang-off position, seabed contact, buoyancy arrangement and internal cross-sectional layout.

The initial structural condition shall include effective tension, axial strain, bending curvature, layer stresses and the equilibrium configuration under submerged weight and buoyancy. Where cross-sectional models are used, the initial contact state between internal components shall be specified.

For a dynamic umbilical, initial displacement and velocity conditions shall correspond to the vessel or platform motion state. Hydraulic tubes shall begin with specified internal pressure, temperature and fluid conditions.

Thermal analysis shall establish the initial temperature of internal tubes, conductors, insulation, armour and surrounding seawater. Fatigue analysis shall include the initial accumulated damage of critical components where available.
Installation simulations shall start from the selected deployment stage, with prescribed suspended length, installation tension, overboarding curvature and seabed touchdown position.
bc: The upper termination shall be constrained to the relevant vessel, platform, hang-off system or subsea structure, with appropriate translation and rotation characteristics. Prescribed host motions shall be transferred to the umbilical connection.

The lower termination shall represent the actual subsea distribution unit, manifold, termination assembly or connection point. It shall include the corresponding translational and rotational stiffness or restraints.

The umbilical exterior shall experience seawater pressure, current loading, wave-induced motion and hydrodynamic forces. At the seabed, contact conditions shall represent friction, embedment resistance and possible separation.

Internal hydraulic tubes shall have pressure and flow boundary conditions appropriate to the hydraulic service. Thermal boundaries shall represent conductor heat generation, hydraulic fluid temperature and heat transfer to ambient seawater.

For bending and crushing analyses, boundaries shall prescribe support curvature, contact loads, imposed deformation or external pressure. Installation boundary conditions shall apply lay tension, vessel motion, deployment speed and overboarding support geometry.

calibration: Calibration should use manufacturer qualification tests, laboratory tensile tests, bending tests, torsion tests, pressure tests, fatigue experiments and measured subsea umbilical response.
Effective axial stiffness, bending stiffness, torsional stiffness and coupling parameters should be calibrated using representative full-cross-section mechanical tests.
Interlayer friction, armour-wire interaction and internal component slip should be calibrated against laboratory bending and tension cycling experiments.
Hydrodynamic drag and added-mass coefficients should be calibrated using oscillatory water-tank tests and measured submerged umbilical motion.
Vessel-induced dynamic response parameters should be informed by measured hang-off motion, tension records and cyclic bending observations.
Seabed contact and friction parameters should be calibrated using representative cable–soil interaction experiments and site-specific geotechnical investigations.
Hydraulic tube pressure-containment behaviour should be calibrated against laboratory pressure tests and manufacturer component qualification data.
Crush and collapse parameters should be informed by external pressure tests and mechanical compression experiments.
Fatigue parameters should be calibrated using representative umbilical cyclic bending and tension tests, including failure observations for critical internal elements.
Thermal expansion and temperature-dependent material behaviour should be informed by controlled thermal cycling experiments.
verification: Global umbilical configuration should be verified using known suspended-line, catenary and beam response benchmarks.
Cross-sectional formulations should be tested against independently calculated axial, bending and torsional stiffness reference cases.
Local stress recovery should be verified through prescribed deformation cases and representative cross-sectional finite-element benchmarks.
Interlayer contact algorithms should undergo convergence testing for friction, contact pressure and relative displacement.
Dynamic umbilical analysis should be checked through modal benchmarks, spatial discretization studies and time-step convergence.
Hydrodynamic loading should be verified under prescribed flow and oscillatory movement.
Minimum bend radius checks should be tested using known geometric curvature cases.
Crush, collapse and tube pressure calculations should be checked against appropriate pressure-vessel and structural benchmarks.
Thermal response should be verified using controlled expansion and heat-transfer reference problems.
Fatigue damage calculations should be tested using reproducible stress histories and independently calculated reference results.
validation: Global shape, tension and curvature should be compared against independent laboratory or full-scale installation measurements.
Cross-sectional stiffness and local stress predictions should be validated using instrumented mechanical testing.
Interlayer slip and frictional behaviour should be assessed against controlled cyclic bending and tensile experiments.
Dynamic response should be compared with measured umbilical motions, tensions and bending histories from laboratory or offshore datasets.
Crush and collapse predictions should be evaluated using independent external pressure tests.
Hydraulic tube integrity should be assessed using pressure qualification tests, leak tests and relevant burst tests.
Fatigue life predictions should be evaluated using representative full-cross-section fatigue experiments and component failure observations.
Thermal expansion and material response should be compared against independently measured thermal cycling behaviour.

Validation must account for the actual internal construction of the umbilical, because different tube, conductor, armour and sheath arrangements can produce substantially different mechanical responses.

geometry.text: Static and dynamic umbilicals, hydraulic tubes, electrical conductors, optical fibre elements, armour wires, strength members, fillers, outer sheaths, buoyancy attachments, termination heads and seabed-laid configurations.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for complete umbilical assemblies, tube cross-sections, helical elements, termination fittings, connectors and supporting components.

DXF profiles, SVG (.svg) vector profiles, STEP cross-sectional solids, IGES curves, Parasolid geometry, and schema-defined CSV, XML or JSON descriptions should be supported for internal component positions, element diameters, layer boundaries, helical lay pitches and cross-sectional arrangement. SVG should be treated as two-dimensional vector geometry requiring appropriate scaling and profile validation before conversion into engineering geometry.

CSV, XYZ, JSON, XML, DXF three-dimensional polylines, GeoJSON, GML and compatible coordinate-based route models should be accepted for static seabed umbilicals, dynamic configurations, touchdown positions and connection paths.

Nastran BDF, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be accepted for compatible global structural models, multilayer cross-sectional analysis, local armour-wire contact and termination assessments.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, LAS/LAZ, E57 and XYZ bathymetric geometry should be supported for irregular touchdown regions, complex seabed profiles, scanned termination hardware and as-installed configurations.
